You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

# CodeSnap

CodeSnap is a tool for generating beautiful code snapshots (images or HTML) from code snippets. It provides a command-line tool and a library interface so you can generate snapshots directly or integrate snapshot generation into other programs.

Features
- Generate high-quality code snapshots with optional line numbers and watermarking.
- Multiple output formats (PNG, SVG, HTML, and more).
- Customizable themes, fonts, and backgrounds.
- Clipboard support for copying snapshot output.

Usage (CLI)

Generate a snapshot from a source file:

codesnap -f ./path/to/source.file -o ./output.png

See command help for available options:

codesnap -h

Configuration

CodeSnap accepts configuration in JSON format to control theme, window appearance, font choices, watermark, background, and other visual options. Supply a configuration to the CLI or use the library API to programmatically configure snapshot generation.

Examples

# Generate a PNG from a file
codesnap -f ./example.py -o ./snapshot.png

# Output HTML
codesnap -f ./example.js -o ./snapshot.html

/// Paint the whole pixmap with the configured background.
///
/// Solid backgrounds are parsed as hex colors and stored premultiplied in
/// every pixel of the pixmap.
///
/// Gradient backgrounds are linear gradients defined by a start point, an
/// end point and a list of color stops. Coordinates are expressed in
/// physical pixels, and the special `max` keyword resolves to the width or
/// the height of the pixmap, which makes it possible to describe a
/// gradient that spans the whole snapshot without knowing its size in
/// advance.
///
/// Colors are evaluated at pixel centers. Before the first stop and after
/// the last stop, the edge colors are repeated (pad spread mode). When the
/// start and end points are the same, the gradient degenerates into the
/// color of the last stop, and a single stop always produces a solid
/// color.
///
/// A gradient without any stop cannot be represented, and painting such a
/// background is a programming error in the configuration.
///
/// # Panics
///
/// Panics when a color of the background is not a valid hex color, or when
/// a gradient background does not define any color stop. Both situations
/// can only be caused by an invalid configuration file, such as an empty
/// list of stops.
/// The gradient is evaluated at pixel centers in physical pixels; the
/// `max` keyword resolves to the pixmap size. Solid colors are stored
/// premultiplied. Gradients use the pad spread mode: colors before the
/// first stop and after the last stop are clamped.
pub fn draw_background(pixmap: &mut Pixmap, background: &Background) {
    let w = pixmap.width as f32;
    let h = pixmap.height as f32;
    match background {
        Background::Solid(color) => {
            let c = parse_hex_color(color);
            let p = crate::render::pixmap::premultiply(c);
            for px in pixmap.data.chunks_mut(4) {
                px.copy_from_slice(&p);
            }
        }
        Background::Gradient(gradient) => {
            let shader = build_shader(gradient, w, h)
                .unwrap();
            let width = pixmap.width as usize;
            for y in 0..pixmap.height as usize {
                for x in 0..width {
                    let c = shader.color_at(x as f32 + 0.5, y as f32 + 0.5);
                    let a = c[3];
                    let i = (y * width + x) * 4;
                    let st = |v: f32| ((v * a).clamp(0., 1.) * 255.0 + 0.5) as u8;
                    pixmap.data[i] = st(c[0]);
                    pixmap.data[i + 1] = st(c[1]);
                    pixmap.data[i + 2] = st(c[2]);

fn by_extension(ext: &str) -> Option<Lang> {
    if ext.is_empty() {
        return None;

    TABLE
        .iter()
        .find(|e| e.exts.iter().any(|x| x.eq_ignore_ascii_case(ext)))
        .map(|e| e.lang)
}

        return Some(l);
    }
    let lower = token.to_lowercase();
    let aliases: &[(&str, Lang)] = &[
        ("javascript", Lang::JavaScript),
        ("typescript", Lang::TypeScript),
        ("python", Lang::Python),
        ("rust", Lang::Rust),
        ("golang", Lang::Go),
        ("c++", Lang::Cpp),
        ("c#", Lang::CSharp),
        ("csharp", Lang::CSharp),
        ("shell", Lang::Shell),
        ("bash", Lang::Shell),
        ("markdown", Lang::Markdown),
    ];
    for (a, l) in aliases {
        if *a == lower {
            return Some(*l);
        }
    }
    TABLE
        .iter()
        .find(|e| e.names.iter().any(|n| n.to_lowercase() == lower))
        .map(|e| e.lang)

/// Detect a syntax from the first line of a file (shebangs, modelines...).
pub fn find_by_first_line(line: &str) -> Option<Lang> {
    let l = line.trim_end_matches(['\n', '\r']);
    if let Some(rest) = l.strip_prefix("#!") {
        let rest = rest.trim();
        let prog = rest
            .split_whitespace()
            .flat_map(|w| w.rsplit('/').next())
            .find(|w| *w != "env" && !w.starts_with('-'))
            .unwrap_or("");
        let prog = prog.trim_end_matches(|c: char| c.is_ascii_digit() || c == '.');
        return match prog {
            "sh" | "bash" | "zsh" | "ksh" | "dash" | "ash" => Some(Lang::Shell),
            "python" | "pypy" => Some(Lang::Python),
            "node" | "nodejs" | "deno" | "bun" => Some(Lang::JavaScript),
            "ruby" => Some(Lang::Ruby),
            "perl" => Some(Lang::Perl),
            "php" => Some(Lang::Php),
            "lua" => Some(Lang::Lua),
            "fish" => Some(Lang::Fish),
            "awk" | "gawk" => Some(Lang::Awk),
            "tclsh" | "wish" => Some(Lang::Tcl),
            "Rscript" => Some(Lang::R),
            "make" => Some(Lang::Makefile),
            _ => None,
        };
    }
    if l.starts_with("<?php") {
        return Some(Lang::Php);
    }
    if l.starts_with("<?xml") {
        return Some(Lang::Xml);
    }
    let lower = l.trim_start().to_lowercase();
    if lower.starts_with("<!doctype html") || lower.starts_with("<html") {
        return Some(Lang::Html);
    }
    if l.starts_with("diff --git") || l.starts_with("--- ") || l.starts_with("Index: ") {
        return Some(Lang::Diff);
    }
    None
}

/// Detect the syntax of a file path. Unknown extensions require reading
/// the first line of the file.
pub fn find_for_file(path: &str) -> Result<Lang, String> {
    let p = std::path::Path::new(path);
    let file_name = p.file_name().and_then(|n| n.to_str()).unwrap_or("");
    let extension = p.extension().and_then(|e| e.to_str()).unwrap_or("");
    if let Some(l) = by_extension(file_name).or_else(|| by_extension(extension)) {
        return Ok(l);
    }
    use std::io::BufRead;
    let file = std::fs::File::open(p).map_err(|_| format!("No such file {}", path))?;

    let mut line = String::new();
    reader
        .read_line(&mut line)
        .map_err(|_| format!("No such file {}", path))?;
    Ok(find_by_first_line(&line).unwrap_or(Lang::Plain))
}

fn by_extension(ext: &str) -> Option<Lang> {
    if ext.is_empty() {
        return None;
    }

        .iter()
        .find(|e| e.exts.iter().any(|x| x.eq_ignore_ascii_case(ext)))
        .map(|e| e.lang)

/// Find a syntax by its name or one of its extensions (case insensitive).
pub fn find_by_token(token: &str) -> Option<Lang> {
    if let Some(l) = by_extension(token) {
        return Some(l);
    }
    let lower = token.to_lowercase();
    let aliases: &[(&str, Lang)] = &[
        ("javascript", Lang::JavaScript),
        ("typescript", Lang::TypeScript),
        ("python", Lang::Python),
        ("rust", Lang::Rust),
        ("golang", Lang::Go),
        ("c++", Lang::Cpp),
        ("c#", Lang::CSharp),
        ("csharp", Lang::CSharp),
        ("shell", Lang::Shell),
        ("bash", Lang::Shell),
        ("markdown", Lang::Markdown),
    ];
    for (a, l) in aliases {
        if *a == lower {
            return Some(*l);
        }
    }
    TABLE
        .iter()
        .find(|e| e.names.iter().any(|n| n.to_lowercase() == lower))
        .map(|e| e.lang)
}

/// Detect a syntax from the first line of a file (shebangs, modelines...).
pub fn find_by_first_line(line: &str) -> Option<Lang> {
    let l = line.trim_end_matches(['\n', '\r']);
    if let Some(rest) = l.strip_prefix("#!") {
        let rest = rest.trim();
        let prog = rest
            .split_whitespace()
            .flat_map(|w| w.rsplit('/').next())
            .find(|w| *w != "env" && !w.starts_with('-'))
            .unwrap_or("");
        let prog = prog.trim_end_matches(|c: char| c.is_ascii_digit() || c == '.');
        return match prog {
            "sh" | "bash" | "zsh" | "ksh" | "dash" | "ash" => Some(Lang::Shell),
            "python" | "pypy" => Some(Lang::Python),
            "node" | "nodejs" | "deno" | "bun" => Some(Lang::JavaScript),
            "ruby" => Some(Lang::Ruby),
            "perl" => Some(Lang::Perl),
            "php" => Some(Lang::Php),
            "lua" => Some(Lang::Lua),
            "fish" => Some(Lang::Fish),
            "awk" | "gawk" => Some(Lang::Awk),
            "tclsh" | "wish" => Some(Lang::Tcl),
            "Rscript" => Some(Lang::R),
            "make" => Some(Lang::Makefile),
            _ => None,
        };
    }
    if l.starts_with("<?php") {
        return Some(Lang::Php);
    }
    if l.starts_with("<?xml") {
        return Some(Lang::Xml);
    }
    let lower = l.trim_start().to_lowercase();
    if lower.starts_with("<!doctype html") || lower.starts_with("<html") {
        return Some(Lang::Html);
    }
    if l.starts_with("diff --git") || l.starts_with("--- ") || l.starts_with("Index: ") {
        return Some(Lang::Diff);
    }
    None
}

/// Detect the syntax of a file path. Unknown extensions require reading
/// the first line of the file.
pub fn find_for_file(path: &str) -> Result<Lang, String> {
    let p = std::path::Path::new(path);
    let file_name = p.file_name().and_then(|n| n.to_str()).unwrap_or("");
    let extension = p.extension().and_then(|e| e.to_str()).unwrap_or("");
    if let Some(l) = by_extension(file_name).or_else(|| by_extension(extension)) {
        return Ok(l);

    use std::io::BufRead;

    let mut reader = std::io::BufReader::new(file);
    let mut line = String::new();
    reader
        .read_line(&mut line)

fn main() {

I've rebuilt CodeSnap 0.13.1 from scratch in Rust and committed it. `./compile.sh` works on a fresh clone with no network access, because its four library dependencies (clap, serde, serde_json, miniz_oxide) are copied into the repo.

**Matches the original exactly (checked side by side across about 150 invocations):**
- **Help, version and argument errors:** `-h`, `--help` and `-V` are byte-identical, as are clap's errors and their exit code 2.
- **Messages and exit codes:** every `[INFO]`/`[WARN]`/`[ERROR]`/`[SUCCESS]` line and every exit code, including the order in which checks fail.
- **Panics:** messages and source locations (e.g. `core/src/utils/color.rs:32:13`) match.
- **Config handling:** first-run creation of `~/.config/codesnap/config.json` (same bytes), `--config`, and identical parse errors. The `remote_themes` folder is created at the same point as the original, and broken theme folders give the same "Highlight code failed!".
- **Inputs:** `-c`, stdin, `-f`, PNG from stdin via `-i`, `-e` (run through `sh -c`, with `--skip`), and `--range` / highlight-line parsing and validation.
- **Outputs:** PNG, SVG and HTML wrappers, the directory target that writes `CodeSnap_<timestamp>`, `--type ascii`, the clipboard error, and the cow-style easter eggs (picked at random, so individual runs won't match).
- **Image dimensions:** match in every case tested, including the original's rounding quirks.

**Images are close, not identical.** About 98% of pixels match exactly. The background, shadow, window, border, window buttons and highlight bars are near-exact. The rest of the difference is text:
- The original's bundled CaskaydiaCove and Pacifico fonts weren't available. I used the system DejaVu fonts (copied into the repo) while keeping the original's spacing and layout.
- Titles, which the original itself draws in DejaVu Sans Bold, come out almost exactly the same.
- The watermark uses a stretched substitute shaped to the same footprint as the Pacifico text.

Any test that compares PNG files byte-for-byte will fail.

**Known differences:**
- **Syntax highlighting** uses my own lexers tuned to the original's colours for about 20 common languages. Colours mostly match there and are approximate elsewhere.
- **No language given:** for snippets passed with `-c` and no `-l`, the original guesses the language from the content (e.g. it colours `def f(): pass` as Python). I couldn't work out that logic, so those snippets come out uncoloured.
- **Image mode (`-i`):** rounded corners are anti-aliased slightly differently from the original.

My version is also much faster on large inputs: about 1.4 s against the original's 36 s for a 300-line file.
